reasons: The source expressly says bundles can pass shipping and fulfillment efficiency to customers while increasing units per transaction, and identifies units per transaction as a major lever for average order value.
The source explicitly recommends using a threshold to make free shipping incentivize customers upward, being specific about its placement, and testing it because thresholds are often set too low.
The candidate correctly identifies $66 as an illustrative, not settled, threshold and retains the source's qualification that it should be dialed in through testing.

The candidate accurately records the source's stated approximately-10% shipping heuristic and appropriately treats it as unresolved because the source uses both cart average order value and total revenue as denominators.
Its limitations accurately reflect that the stated evidence is the speaker's own 2019–2020 tests and that the excerpt supplies no test design, sample, or definition of material conversion impact.
The source's worked example specifically describes a one-click cart upgrade from the serum to the routine, adding the cleanser and recovery night cream.
It also supports the stated framing: the single-item purchaser lacks the gift and free shipping and is shown the routine as a way to obtain those benefits and savings.
The source explicitly favors incentivizing image and video reviews subject to legality and compliance in the country of advertising, and gives a $10 next-order gift-card example.
The candidate preserves the source's asserted distinction between directly paying for reviews and providing incentives, including the jurisdictional limitation and the image-review cash-back example.
The source directly advises choosing gifts with low merchant cost and high perceived value.
The candidate accurately labels the $30-priced, roughly $4–$5-cost ritual set and the over-$60 order threshold as details of the example rather than general numerical requirements.
The source expressly says traffic can be sent directly to the routine page while continuing to be sent to the single serum page.
It supports the dependency on the cart upgrade, since the source says the cart displayed after adding the single product is where visitors can add the routine.

omissions.description: The excerpt separately asserts an outcome for using a gift with purchase: improving break-even ROAS. The candidates address gift selection and thresholds but do not represent this claimed effect.
omissions.quote: The gift with purchase improves break even rorowaz.

source_limitations: The excerpt begins mid-sentence and ends mid-sentence, so adjacent context that could qualify the opening claim and the final proof example is missing.

Several quantitative and performance claims are attributed only to the speaker's experience with their own e-commerce stores in 2019–2020; the excerpt provides no sample sizes, product categories, controls, test design, or measurements.
The $122 bundle, $14 discount, $60 gift threshold, $66 shipping threshold, and post-checkout offer are presented as a worked example. The excerpt does not establish that those values generalize.
Legal and compliance statements about review incentives are described broadly and jurisdictionally, without identifying applicable jurisdictions, rules, or disclosure requirements.

Uh, bundles work really well because they allow you to pass on the shipping and fulfillment efficiency to the customer while pushing up units per transaction, which is one of the biggest levers that underpins average order value. And then there's two additional levers that no one really talks about properly, which is shipping. Free shipping is not always the win that it looks like because it teaches the customer to value delivery separately from the product. And shipping collected is almost pure profit for most people. Most people can charge shipping up to about 10% of the average order value of the cart. And it won't impact conversion rate at all. And I ran a lot of tests myself on my own e-commerce stores back in 2019 2020 on this. I did a lot of free shipping testing, introducing shipping back in, putting shipping insurance, putting expedited shipping, all of these different options. And generally speaking, as long as you keep your shipping collected at sub 10% of total revenue, it has no material impact on conversion rates. And so if you're going to give away free shipping, you definitely want to give it away at a threshold to incentivize people up. And then if you're going to do it at a threshold, you want to be very specific as to where you place that threshold and do a lot of testing around it because most people set their free shipping threshold way too low. Now the second lever that exists is the post-purchase upsell. Right after they buy, one click, no re-entering their card. You can just bill them a second time with a oneclick upsell. It obviously has to be relevant to what they just bought, not a random add-on, but it's the cleanest, easiest way to increase average order value because you're presenting it right as they're the warmest within the entire funnel because they've just spent money and you hit them with obviously a discount on that cross-eller upsell. Ends up having a very high take rate, increases revenue per visitor. So now going back to our example, we have a bad offer on the left, a good offer on the right, honing in on the left, we've got a 20% off. Obviously, this is going to erode margin enormously. It's just lazy discounting. It's not increasing average order value. This is what most people do. Revenue is going to go up, sure, but profit is going to go down here. Now, this is also going to train the customer to wait for discounts. People that start doing 20% off everything discounts pretty quickly. Everyone knows them for doing 20% off everything discounts and they can't get out of this rut and so they become reliant on it. Now, we have a good offer on the right. There's a lot going on here, but this is what the best direct to consumer brands are doing at the moment. So, we've moved away from the overnight repair serum, and we've moved into a routine bundle. The bundle has a gentle cleanser, overnight repair serum, and then the recovery night cream. And each of these is framed as a different step. And so, you need each of these steps to actually be able to achieve the outcome that you're after. Immediately by doing this, it's increased our average order value to $122. Now, what we've also done is we've baked in a discount across the bundle. Now, the discount that we're giving is $14. So, normally this is valued at $136, but we're going to give it for $122. We lose no margin here because we are just passing on our economies of scale from shipping these three items together. If we were to ship them separately, we would have to pay shipping and fulfillment costs three separate times, which would have cost us an additional $14. But shipping them together, we save on the duplication of shipping fees. Therefore, our margin is the same. We don't actually lose any margin giving this discount away. We're also going to give away free shipping at 66. Now, this would need to be really thoughtful as to do we really want it at 66, do we want it a little bit higher? We'd obviously need to dial this in, test it over time, but we've got a free shipping offer there. But then really the key of this whole landing page is that yes, we can drive traffic straight to the routine page, but we can continue driving traffic to just the overnight repair serum. When people click add to cart, this is what appears in the cart. They haven't achieved free [snorts] shipping yet. We're happy to give away the $14 here because we're actually saving on shipping and fulfillment cost by shipping this all together. The free gift is $4 and so the margin impact is very minimal.
